phonemes.desc: Initial velar [ɡ] followed by short, open [ɐ] — the soft ground from which the name rises.
Retroflex nasal [ɳ] plus long [eː], a resonant, elevated syllable that distinguishes Gaṇeśa from common gana.
Palatal sibilant [ɕ] (not retroflex [ʂ]) plus short [ɐ] — the śakti of sound and auspiciousness.

pronunciation.approximation: 'guh-NAH-shuh' — say the second syllable with a bright, held 'ay' sound and a soft, tongue-tip n.

kin.label: Sanskrit
kin.form: गणेश (Gaṇeśa), from gaṇa ('troop, host, category') + īśa ('lord, master') — Monier-Williams s.v.

kin.label: Vedic root
kin.form: gaṇ- appears already in the Ṛgveda for divine hosts; īśa is the sovereign power behind a thing

kin.label: Tamil/Marathi kin
kin.form: Pillaiyar / Gaṇapati — the same figure refracted through regional phonology and devotion

pronunciation.note: Gaṇeśa is Tier 1 because the restoration preserves the retroflex ṇ and palatal ś plus the inherently long e — distinctive sounds and vowel length that ASCII 'Ganesha' flattens entirely. In IAST no macron ever appears on e or o, which are always long in Sanskrit.

domains.title: Lord of Beginnings and Obstacles
domains.lead: Gaṇeśa is the doorway-god of the Hindu pantheon. No ritual, wedding, venture, or text is properly begun until he has been honored, for he holds the keys to vighna — the obstacles that cluster at every threshold. Yet he is more than a divine doorman: he is the patron of learning, the scribe of epic poetry, and the sovereign of the gaṇas, the unruly hosts who serve Śiva.

cards.name: Wisdom & Learning
cards.desc: Gaṇeśa is buddhi-siddhi, the lord of discernment; students invoke him before examinations and scholars before writing.

cards.name: Beginnings & Thresholds
cards.desc: Every new undertaking — a house, a book, a marriage — begins with Gaṇapati pūjā, sealing the threshold against ill fortune.

cards.name: Obstacle-Removal
cards.desc: As Vighneśvara he both places and removes obstacles; his axe cuts through the inner and outer impediments to dharma.

cards.name: Lord of the Gaṇas
cards.desc: He commands the divine hosts, transforming chaos into ordered retinue; his sovereignty is over categories themselves.

symbols.name: Elephant head
symbols.meaning: Wisdom, memory, and the power to uproot obstacles — the head Śiva gave him after striking off the first

symbols.name: Broken tusk
symbols.meaning: Sacrifice for the sake of scripture; Gaṇeśa is said to have used it as a stylus to write the Mahābhārata

symbols.name: Mouse vāhana
symbols.meaning: Desire and ego brought under control; the tiny mount shows that wisdom governs even the most restless impulses

symbols.name: Modaka sweet
symbols.meaning: The rewards of spiritual practice — sweet, but earned through discipline

symbols.name: Axe (paraśu)
symbols.meaning: The power to sever attachment and cut away the roots of obstacle

mythology.lead: Gaṇeśa's myths are the theology of thresholds: a boy made by his mother, beheaded by his father, and reborn with an elephant's head; a race lost by the fast and won by the devout; a mouse ridden like a lesson. Every story ends at a doorway — with wisdom, patience, or a well-placed curse standing guard.

myths.title: Born of Turmeric and Devotion
myths.text: While Pārvatī bathed, she shaped a boy from the turmeric paste and unguents rubbed from her own body and set him at her door with orders to let no one in. Śiva returned, was stopped, and an argument became a battle; Śiva's trident struck off the boy's head (Śiva Purāṇa, Rudrasaṃhitā 2.13–18; the Liṅga Purāṇa tells the same core story). Pārvatī's grief summoned armies of goddesses and nearly unmade the three worlds; to appease her, Śiva sent his gaṇas to bring the head of the first creature found facing north — they returned with an elephant's head — and restored the boy, declaring him his own son and granting him precedence at every beginning. The household myth carries a complete theology: the child made by the mother alone is legitimate, the father's violence is repaired by fatherhood, and the new head — elephantine, wise, unforgetting — makes the boy instantly recognizable across languages and regions. Gaṇeśa is born from the union of error and repair, which is to say, from family life itself.

myths.title: Around the World or Around the Parents
myths.text: Śiva set his two sons a contest: circle the world, and the winner takes the fruit of knowledge. Skanda — Kārttikeya, the war-god — leapt instantly onto his peacock and vanished over the horizon. Gaṇeśa, on his tiny mouse, had not the speed to compete; instead he rose, walked once slowly around his seated parents, and returned. Asked what he had done, he answered that his parents were his whole world — and Śiva awarded him the prize (the story is told in the Purāṇic tradition, notably in the Skanda Purāṇa cycle, and endlessly retold in regional literature). The nimble brother loses to the one who redefines the race: not the circumference of the earth but the circle of love is the measure of a world. The myth doubles as Gaṇeśa's charter for precedence — invoked first at beginnings — and as one of Hinduism's gentlest arguments that devotion outruns performance. It also quietly sorts the brothers' domains: Skanda, god of war and distance; Gaṇeśa, god of doorways and return.

myths.title: The Mouse as Mount
myths.text: Gaṇeśa's mount is a mouse — muṣika — and the tradition does not let the absurdity pass unexamined. In one account the mouse began as a demon, Muṣikasura, who gnawed through scriptures and granaries until Gaṇeśa subdued him and, instead of destroying him, took him as a vehicle (the tale belongs to the Gaṇeśa Purāṇa and the Mudgala Purāṇa cycles). The symbolism is deliberately homely: the mouse is desire — small, quick, endlessly gnawing, always hungry — and the vast elephant-headed god rides it to show that wisdom does not destroy appetite but seats itself upon it. India's greatest temples and its smallest grain-stores share the same theology: what you cannot exterminate, you must learn to ride. The mouse beneath Gaṇeśa is the mind beneath the meditator, and the god's comfortable seat is the tradition's image of what mastery looks like when it is no longer a struggle.

myths.title: The Scribe of the Mahābhārata
myths.text: When Vyāsa needed a scribe for the Mahābhārata — the longest poem in the world — he chose Gaṇeśa, who agreed on one condition: the dictation must never pause. Vyāsa countered with his own condition: Gaṇeśa must understand every verse before writing it (Mahābhārata, Ādi Parvan 1, vulgate recension). So began the epic's great race: the sage composing at the edge of comprehension, the god writing at the edge of speed. And in the famous detail, Gaṇeśa's stylus wore down and, unwilling to break his promise, he snapped off his own tusk and wrote on with it. The broken tusk became his emblem — the god who paid a piece of himself for the text's sake — and the epic acquired a patron deity of scholarship. The myth frames all writing as a vow between two parties, each holding the other to greatness: the teacher who must never stop, the student who must never stop understanding. Every examination hall in India invokes the tusk-broken scribe for exactly this reason.

myths.title: The Curse That Made the Fortnight
myths.text: One night after a feast, Gaṇeśa rode his mouse home beneath a full moon, and when the mouse startled at a snake and threw him, the moon — Soma, proud of his beauty — laughed at the pot-bellied god sprawled in the dust. Gaṇeśa cursed him: whoever looks at you shall be falsely accused and lose his good name (the story is told in the Gaṇeśa Purāṇa's Kṛḍā-khaṇḍa). The moon's radiance was eaten away, the gods begged mercy, and Gaṇeśa relented — but kept a lesson in the sky: the dark fortnight is the curse's remainder, and moon-gazing on his own festival remains taboo. The myth explains the lunar month and the etiquette of Gaṇeśa Caturthī in a single stroke, and its moral is a god-sized version of a household truth: laughter at another's fall is the one debt the heavens always collect. Even the moon, who shines on everything, was taught what it costs to shine on someone's shame.

lore.syncretism: Gaṇeśa has absorbed and been absorbed by countless regional deities. In Jainism, he appears as a yakṣa and remover of obstacles; in Buddhism, especially in Tibet and Nepal, he is adopted as a protector and wealth-bestower under names such as Vināyaka. Southeast Asian kingdoms — Champa, Khmer, Javanese — carried his cult across the Indian Ocean, where he merged with local guardian spirits. In Maharashtra, he becomes the people's god during Gaṇeśa Caturthī; in Tamil country, he is Pillaiyar, the noble child. Even his mother-centric origin story balances the fierce, world-renouncing Śiva with the domestic, creative power of Pārvatī, making Gaṇeśa a bridge between ascetic and household religion.
lore.culturalLegacy: Gaṇeśa is arguably the most universally recognized Hindu deity in the world. His image opens businesses, books, films, and computer screens; his mantra, Oṃ Gaṃ Gaṇapataye Namaḥ, is chanted at inaugurations from Mumbai to Silicon Valley. The annual Gaṇeśa Caturthī transforms cities into rivers of song and procession, culminating in the immersion of clay images. In modern India, he has become a symbol of cultural unity and environmental awareness, with devotees increasingly returning his idols to biodegradable forms. From comic books to corporate logos, Gaṇeśa endures as the friendly face of the divine — the god who removes obstacles because he has already overcome the greatest one: being different.
lore.extendedMeditation:
To meditate on Gaṇeśa is to meditate on thresholds. Every doorway is a decision: to enter or to turn back, to speak or to remain silent, to begin or to postpone. Gaṇeśa sits at that edge, his large ears listening to the unspoken fear, his small eyes focused on the single task ahead. The obstacle is rarely what it appears. More often it is the tremor of the mind before action — the mouse of doubt scratching at the foundations.

His elephant head teaches memory: remember what you have already survived. His broken tusk teaches sacrifice: every great work costs something. His mouse teaches discipline: the smallest impulse, once governed, becomes a vehicle. Beginnings are sacred because they are rehearsals of freedom. Gaṇeśa does not promise that the path will be easy; he promises that the path can be taken.
lore.originalScriptNote: The Devanagari form is गणेश. In IAST transliteration, dots beneath consonants (ṇ, ṣ) indicate retroflex articulation; e and o are always long in Sanskrit and are never macroned. The name is often spelled Gaṇapati (गणपति) in older texts, with the same root gaṇa ('host, troop').

lore.archaeology: The earliest independent Gaṇeśa images date to the Gupta period: the Udayagiri caves (c. 401 CE), Bhumara, and Nachna show the elephant-headed deity. Gupta terracottas from Ahichchhatra and Rajghat spread his icon across the Gangetic plain. Ellora and Elephanta preserve medieval sculptures, and Badami's Chalukyan caves include early relief panels. Dvāravatī and Khmer art carried his image into Southeast Asia as a Tantric protector.
